headline: North Carolina cannabis council told by Oklahoma: keep licences tight
dek: An Oklahoma narcotics official urged North Carolina's cannabis advisers to license as tightly as possible before the council's last meeting on 17 November.
key_points: Lt. Col. Mitch Smith of the Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics told a North Carolina advisory subcommittee on 12 November that Oklahoma's open-ended medical licensing led to overproduction, straw ownership and illegal operators.
Oklahoma had 8,400 commercial growers by 2021 with no cap on plants or licences, and spends about $10 million a year on 48 marijuana enforcement agents and analysts, Smith said.
The full North Carolina Advisory Council on Cannabis meets on 17 November, its expected last meeting before it sends recommendations to Gov. Josh Stein in December.
In Asheville on 14 November, hemp businesses gathered petition signatures against the federal 0.4mg THC cap due on 11 December, the products North Carolina's council was set up to regulate.
body: North Carolina's cannabis advisers heard a blunt warning from Oklahoma this week: license as tightly as you can, or spend years cleaning up afterwards. Lt. Col. Mitch Smith, who runs the marijuana enforcement unit of the Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs, told the Public Safety Subcommittee of the North Carolina Advisory Council on Cannabis on 12 November that his state's medical program, approved by voters eight years ago, produced a string of problems it never planned for, NC Newsline reported in a story republished by Marijuana Moment on 14 November.

The timing matters. The full council, created by Gov. Josh Stein in June 2025, meets on 17 November in Raleigh in what is expected to be its last session before it delivers final recommendations to the governor in December. Those recommendations will shape the first serious attempt to bring North Carolina's large, unregulated intoxicating hemp market and a possible legal cannabis market under one set of rules.

Smith described three failures. First, ownership. Oklahoma required that 75% of any medical marijuana business be owned by state residents, but out-of-state operators found local residents willing to act as straw owners for a fee, he said, and the real operators were often bad actors or foreign nationals. His bureau knows of 27 groups from at least 16 countries operating illegally in the state, he told the subcommittee.

Second, supply. Oklahoma set no limit on the number of licences or on how much a licensee could grow. By 2021 it had 8,400 commercial growers, Smith said, and the overproduction fed the illicit market. Third, cleanup. Agents now deal with abandoned grow houses, waste and banned pesticides that could contaminate well water, and Smith said he feared the state would end up paying to restore the land.

The cost is ongoing. Oklahoma spends about $10 million a year on 48 agents and analysts dedicated to marijuana enforcement, according to Smith. His agents seized more than 50,000 illegal plants last week alone, he said, and the courts had to find Mandarin and Cantonese interpreters and write jury instructions in those languages for defendants who did not speak English. His one recommendation, he said, was to make licensing as restrictive as possible.
> Oklahoma is the cautionary tale every new market now hears: cheap, unlimited licences bring in the operators regulators least want.

Rosanna Smart, co-director of the RAND Drug Policy Research Center, gave the subcommittee a more measured picture. North Carolina may spend more on enforcement in the first years after legalization, she said, but research shows a legal market can take a large share from the illicit one, because consumers will pay higher prices for products they trust to be tested and accurately labelled.

She added a caveat that fits North Carolina closely: most of the evidence comes from early-adopting states, not from places where cannabis is still illegal but intoxicating hemp products are already sold everywhere. That is exactly North Carolina's position, and it is the problem the council was told to solve. The state's own description of the council says the governor charged it with designing a system that protects young people, allows adult sales, supports agriculture, expunges past convictions for simple THC possession and directs revenue to addiction, mental health and drugged-driving programmes.
## The hemp shops already in business

The pressure from the hemp side is building too. On 14 November, Asheville hemp businesses held a community gathering and petition drive against the federal limit of 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container that takes effect on 11 December, WLOS reported. Franny's Farmacy chief executive Franny Tacy, who hosted, said the cap would put retailers out of business and hurt farmers and consumers. A local hemp grower told the station the industry was open to regulation but that the federal change would shut it down. State Sen. Julie Mayfield attended and said she wanted Congress to replace the cap with reasonable rules, starting with age limits.

That leaves North Carolina in an unusual spot. Federal law is about to remove most of the hemp products the council was formed to regulate, while the state has no licensed cannabis market to absorb the demand. Oklahoma's lesson, as Smith told it, is that opening the door too wide is hard to undo; the hemp shops' lesson is that closing it entirely pushes existing businesses out.

Any recommendations would still need the General Assembly. House Speaker-elect Robert Reives, whose Democrats take control of the chamber in 2027, said this week that his caucus wants to explore decriminalization, as we reported on 10 November. The council's report will be advice, not law, and lawmakers can take or leave its licensing model.

The full council meets from 1:30 to 5 p.m. on 17 November at the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services in Raleigh. Watch whether its draft licensing recommendations include caps on licence numbers or canopy, residency rules, and how it proposes to treat existing hemp retailers. The final report goes to Gov. Stein in December. On 11 December, the federal hemp cap takes effect unless Congress changes it in the year-end funding bill, and North Carolina's hemp shops will find out whether they still have a product to sell. The legislative session that opens in January is where any of it becomes law.
